description: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins, key minerals, antioxidants, and the vital role of hydration.
content_html:
Micronutrients — The Small but Essential Nutrients

Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in tiny quantities — milligrams or micrograms rather than grams. Unlike macronutrients, they do not supply energy; instead they regulate countless body processes, from bone formation to immune defence to energy release from food. Missing even one regularly causes a specific deficiency disease. The exam expects you to know each one’s functions, main sources, and effects of deficiency and excess.

Fat-Soluble Vitamins

Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and body fat, so they do not need to be eaten every day — but they can build up to toxic levels if consumed in very high doses (excess). There are four: A, D, E and K.

  • Vitamin A — needed for vision in dim light (rhodopsin production), healthy skin, and immune function. Sources: liver, oily fish, dairy, eggs; also from beta-carotene in orange and yellow vegetables (carrots, sweet potato, butternut squash). Deficiency causes night blindness and dry skin.
  • Vitamin D — essential for absorbing calcium and phosphorus, so it underpins strong bones and teeth. The body makes it when skin is exposed to sunlight; dietary sources include oily fish, eggs, fortified cereals and fortified spreads. Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults (soft, painful bones).
  • Vitamin E — an antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage. Sources include vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and avocado. Deficiency is rare in healthy adults but can cause nerve damage.
  • Vitamin K — essential for blood clotting and bone health. Main sources: green leafy vegetables (kale, spinach, broccoli), vegetable oils, fermented foods. Deficiency causes impaired blood clotting.
Key Fact

Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are stored in the liver and body fat. Excess can be toxic. Deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets in children; deficiency of vitamin A causes night blindness.

Water-Soluble Vitamins — The B Group and Vitamin C

Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in water and cannot be stored in large amounts, so they need to be eaten regularly. They are also easily lost during food preparation and cooking — a critical exam point.

  • B1 (thiamin) — needed for energy release from carbohydrates. Sources: pork, fortified cereals, nuts, peas. Deficiency causes beriberi (nerve damage, muscle weakness).
  • B2 (riboflavin) — supports energy metabolism and healthy skin. Sources: milk, eggs, liver, fortified cereals.
  • B3 (niacin) — needed for energy metabolism and DNA repair. Sources: meat, fish, peanuts, fortified flour. Severe deficiency causes pellagra.
  • Folic acid (folate) — essential for making new red blood cells and for healthy fetal development (prevents neural tube defects). Sources: green leafy vegetables, beans, fortified bread. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia; pregnant women are advised to supplement.
  • B12 (cobalamin) — required for red blood cell formation and maintaining the nervous system. Sources: meat, fish, dairy, eggs (virtually absent from non-fortified plant foods). Deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and nerve damage; vegans must supplement or eat fortified foods.
  • Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) — needed for collagen synthesis (skin, blood vessels, wound healing), immune function, and iron absorption from plant foods. Sources: fresh fruit (oranges, kiwi, strawberries), peppers, broccoli, potatoes. Deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, slow wound healing).

Vitamins C and the B-group are water-soluble and heat-sensitive, so they leach into cooking water and are destroyed by prolonged heat. When you boil broccoli, the vitamin C and folate dissolve into the water — which is then poured down the drain. To minimise losses: use the minimum water possible; steam rather than boil (the food doesn’t sit in water); use short cooking times; prepare vegetables just before cooking (chopping increases surface area and speeds up oxidation); avoid keeping cooked vegetables warm for long periods. These facts are frequently tested with a “describe” command word.

Key Minerals

The spec lists six minerals you must know: calcium, iron, sodium, fluoride, iodine and phosphorus.

  • Calcium — builds and maintains bones and teeth, assists muscle contraction and nerve function. Sources: milk, cheese, yoghurt, fortified plant milks, canned fish with bones (sardines), dark green vegetables. Deficiency causes rickets (children) or osteoporosis (adults).
  • Iron — needed for making haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells. Sources: red meat (haem iron, absorbed most efficiently), liver, fortified cereals, lentils, dark green vegetables. Deficiency causes iron-deficiency anaemia (fatigue, pale skin, breathlessness). Vitamin C consumed at the same meal increases non-haem iron absorption from plant foods.
  • Sodium (salt) — regulates fluid balance and nerve impulses. Too much raises blood pressure (hypertension), increasing the risk of stroke and CHD. Most dietary sodium comes from processed foods. The Reference Intake for adults is 2.4 g sodium (6 g salt) per day.
  • Fluoride — strengthens tooth enamel and reduces tooth decay. Sources: fluoridated water, tea, fish. Excess causes dental fluorosis (mottled teeth).
  • Iodine — essential for making thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism. Sources: milk, dairy, seafood, some fortified foods. Deficiency causes goitre (enlarged thyroid gland) and, in pregnancy, can impair the baby’s brain development.
  • Phosphorus — works alongside calcium to build bones and teeth; also involved in energy metabolism. Sources: meat, fish, dairy, eggs, cereals.
Key Fact

Iron makes haemoglobin to carry oxygen in blood. Deficiency causes iron-deficiency anaemia. Calcium builds bones and teeth; deficiency causes rickets (children) or osteoporosis (adults). Vitamin C increases absorption of non-haem iron from plant sources.

Antioxidants — Protecting Cells from Damage

Antioxidants neutralise free radicals — unstable molecules that damage cell membranes and DNA. The three antioxidant vitamins on the spec are:

  • Vitamin A (from beta-carotene in plant foods) — protects cells in the respiratory and digestive tracts.
  • Vitamin C — water-soluble antioxidant; active in the fluid inside cells and in blood plasma.
  • Vitamin E — fat-soluble antioxidant; embedded in cell membranes where it prevents oxidative damage to fats.

Eating a diet rich in colourful fruits and vegetables — a Greek salad of tomatoes, peppers, cucumber and olive oil, or a fruit salad of kiwi, strawberries and orange — provides a wide range of antioxidants. This is part of the evidence base behind the government’s five-a-day guidance.

Many students incorrectly state that all vitamins are lost when you boil vegetables. Only water-soluble vitamins (B-group and C) leach into cooking water. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) do not dissolve in water and are not lost by boiling — though they can be damaged by prolonged very high heat. The practical implication is: to preserve vitamin C in a stir-fry, use high heat for a short time with very little water; to preserve vitamin C in boiled broccoli, steam instead and serve immediately.

Water and Hydration

Water is not classified as a macronutrient or micronutrient but is essential for life. Its key functions are: transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood; removing waste products as urine; regulating body temperature through sweating; acting as a lubricant in joints; and supporting digestion. The body loses water through breathing, sweating, urinating and in faeces. Adults should drink approximately 6–8 cups (around 1.5–2 litres) of fluid per day. More is needed in hot weather, during exercise, and when ill. Dehydration causes headaches, fatigue, reduced concentration and, in severe cases, organ failure.
exam_tip_html: When a question uses the command word Describe, examiners expect at least two or three distinct points with relevant characteristics for each. A common mistake with micronutrients is naming a vitamin without pairing it with its function, source or deficiency effect — that earns only 1 of 3 marks. For example, “Vitamin C prevents scurvy” is one point. Add “good sources include citrus fruit and peppers” and “it is water-soluble and is lost when vegetables are boiled in water” and you have three distinct marks. For the 6-mark Explain extended response, remember that water-soluble vitamins and their preservation in cooking is a high-tariff topic — make sure you can explain not just which vitamins are lost but why (they dissolve in cooking water and are destroyed by heat).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) are needed in small amounts and do not supply energy. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in the body; excess can be toxic. Water-soluble vitamins (B-group and C) cannot be stored and are easily lost during cooking.
  • Key antioxidant vitamins are A, C and E — they neutralise free radicals and protect body cells from damage. Colourful fruits and vegetables supply the broadest range of antioxidants.
  • Water is essential for transport, waste removal, temperature regulation and digestion. Adults need approximately 6–8 cups of fluid per day; requirements increase with exercise, heat and illness.

practice_questions.text:
Which vitamin is produced in the skin when exposed to sunlight and is essential for calcium absorption?
A. Vitamin A
B. Vitamin C
C. Vitamin D
D. Vitamin K
Give two reasons why water-soluble vitamins are often lost when vegetables are boiled.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: the vitamins dissolve into the cooking water; the vitamins are destroyed/broken down by heat; the longer the cooking time, the greater the loss. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the functions of vitamin C in the body and identify two good dietary sources.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any three distinct points from: needed for collagen synthesis (skin, blood vessels, wound healing); supports immune function; acts as an antioxidant (neutralises free radicals/protects cells from damage); increases absorption of non-haem iron from plant foods. Plus 1 mark each for two named sources (e.g. oranges, kiwi, strawberries, peppers, broccoli, potatoes). Up to 3 marks total — any three distinct points from functions and sources combined.

practice_questions.text: Theo is a 16-year-old vegetarian who rarely eats dairy products. His GP has raised concerns about his vitamin D and calcium intake. Explain why Theo is at risk and suggest two ways he could improve his intake of both nutrients.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks available per developed point. (1) Vitamin D: Theo is at risk because dairy (milk, yoghurt, cheese) is a key dietary source of vitamin D; without it, absorption of calcium will also be reduced because vitamin D is needed for calcium uptake. He could improve intake by spending time outdoors (sunlight triggers skin synthesis of vitamin D) or eating fortified foods such as plant milks and fortified cereals. (2) Calcium: without dairy, major sources of calcium are removed from his diet; deficiency can lead to poor bone density and increased risk of osteoporosis. He could eat canned fish with bones (sardines), dark green leafy vegetables (kale, broccoli), or fortified plant milks. 1 mark for identification of risk; 1 mark for developed explanation or practical solution per point.

practice_questions.text: Name two antioxidant vitamins and describe how antioxidants protect body cells.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two correctly named antioxidant vitamins (Vitamin A / Vitamin C / Vitamin E — any two); 1 mark for explaining that antioxidants neutralise free radicals (unstable molecules) which would otherwise damage cell membranes and DNA. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Sienna is a student nurse who wants to plan a week of packed lunches that preserve water-soluble vitamins as much as possible. She often prepares lunches the evening before and takes vegetables raw or cooked. Explain how Sienna should prepare, store and choose her food to maximise water-soluble vitamin content, linking your answer to the chemistry of vitamin loss.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Explains at least two mechanisms of vitamin loss (dissolving into cooking water; destroyed by heat; oxidation when cut surfaces are exposed to air) and links each to a specific practical strategy (steam or stir-fry rather than boil; prepare vegetables just before eating rather than overnight; store in a sealed container in a cool place to minimise oxidation; include raw salad vegetables such as peppers and tomatoes; choose vitamin-C-rich foods that can be eaten raw). Accurately identifies B-group and vitamin C as the affected vitamins. Sustained, well-developed reasoning chains using correct terminology.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one mechanism and two practical strategies. Generally accurate. Some development of reasoning.

Developing (2 marks): Names water-soluble vitamins and suggests a practical tip but without explaining the underlying reason, or gives a general statement about cooking destroying vitamins without specifying which ones or how.

Emerging (1 mark): Very limited response, e.g. 'cook vegetables quickly' with no explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following minerals is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells?
Vitamin B12 is found mainly in animal products. Which group is most at risk of B12 deficiency?
Vitamins A, D, E and K are _____ vitamins, meaning they are stored in the liver and body fat.
Deficiency of vitamin D in children causes _____, a condition where bones become soft and deformed.
Match each nutrient with its deficiency effect.
right: Scurvy — bleeding gums and slow wound healing
Iron-deficiency anaemia — fatigue and pale skin

flashcard_questions.q: What are micronutrients and how do they differ from macronutrients?
flashcard_questions.a: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts; they do not supply energy.
Vitamins A, D, E, K — stored in the liver and body fat, excess can reach toxic levels.

flashcard_questions.q: What is vitamin D needed for and what happens if a child is deficient?
flashcard_questions.a: Calcium absorption and bone health; deficiency causes rickets.

flashcard_questions.q: What is vitamin C (ascorbic acid) needed for?
flashcard_questions.a: Collagen formation, immune function and absorbing non-haem iron from plant foods.

flashcard_questions.q: What condition is caused by vitamin C deficiency?
flashcard_questions.a: Scurvy — characterised by bleeding gums and slow wound healing.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must vegans supplement or eat fortified foods for vitamin B12?
flashcard_questions.a: B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products; deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are water-soluble vitamins lost when vegetables are boiled?
flashcard_questions.a: They dissolve into the cooking water and are broken down by heat.

flashcard_questions.q: Which cooking method best preserves water-soluble vitamins in vegetables?
flashcard_questions.a: Steaming — the vegetables do not sit in water.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three antioxidant vitamins on the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Vitamins A, C, E — each neutralises free radicals in different cellular environments.

flashcard_questions.q: What do antioxidants do in the body?
flashcard_questions.a: They neutralise free radicals, protecting cell membranes and DNA from oxidative damage.

flashcard_questions.q: What does calcium do in the body and what foods supply it?
flashcard_questions.a: Builds bones and teeth; found in dairy, fortified plant milks and dark green vegetables.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does vitamin C eaten at a meal increase iron absorption?
flashcard_questions.a: It converts non-haem iron into a form the body can absorb more easily from plant foods.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main function of water in the body?
flashcard_questions.a: Transporting nutrients and waste, regulating body temperature and supporting digestion.

glossary_terms.definition: Nutrients needed in small amounts that do not supply energy; they include vitamins, minerals and trace elements.
Vitamins A, D, E and K, which dissolve in fat, are stored in the liver and body fat, and can accumulate to toxic levels if taken in excess.
Vitamins B-group and C, which dissolve in water, cannot be stored in large amounts, and are easily lost during cooking.
Highly reactive molecules produced during normal body metabolism; in excess they damage cells and DNA and are linked to chronic disease.
Substances, including vitamins A, C and E, that neutralise free radicals and protect body cells from oxidative damage.
